passage: Counsellor's note, Monday. Sangeeta stood up in Mr Rao's class today and said the assigned seating made group work slower, and that the rule had been made without asking anyone. Her voice was firm and her hands were on her desk. The class went quiet. Mr Rao asked her to stay after the bell and she sat down with her arms crossed. In our meeting I did not defend the rule. I asked what she wanted to be different. After a minute she said she wanted a say, even for one week in the month. She also said she does not want to be seen as rude. I will take her request to the staff meeting and tell her what they decide. Lakshmi.

qa.q: Whose class was Sangeeta in when she disputed the seating rule?
qa.a: She was in Mr Rao's class.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta seem to want underneath her challenge?
qa.a: She seems to want a voice and some respect in decisions that affect her, and she worries about being seen as rude. The firm voice could also mean she was simply frustrated about slow group work.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped?
qa.a: The counsellor asked what Sangeeta wanted to be different instead of defending the rule, and promised to bring the request to staff and report back. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mr Rao have felt when Sangeeta stood up?
qa.a: He may have felt challenged in front of the class, or possibly surprised, which could be why he asked her to stay after the bell.

grounding: A teen disputes a rule to build independence, and the adult listens for the request underneath.

passage:
Sunday night, 10:40.

Today I told Mummy that the 9 pm phone rule was unfair. I said it in front of Pallavi masi too, which was maybe a mistake. My voice went loud. I said everyone in my class keeps their phone till eleven, and that I do my homework on time. Mummy said that wasn't the point. I said then what is the point, and she just looked at me.

Then Pallavi masi said, "Himani, what do you want, exactly?" I said, I want to be trusted with my own time. Mummy went quiet and said we can try 10 pm for two weeks.

I still feel a bit shaky. But it felt good to say it. 🙂

qa.q: Which rule did Himani call unfair?
qa.a: Himani called the 9 pm phone rule unfair.

qa.q: Why did Himani ask to be trusted with her own time?
qa.a: Under the argument, Himani wants independence and some respect for handling homework well. Himani might also have been embarrassed about arguing in front of Pallavi masi.

qa.q: What worked in how the adults responded?
qa.a: Pallavi masi asked what Himani really wanted, and Mummy agreed to a two-week trial, which turned the argument into a request.

qa.q: How might Himani's mother feel after this talk?
qa.a: She may feel unsettled by the challenge, yet also relieved that Himani explained her wish calmly in the end.

grounding: A teenager disputes a phone rule to gain independence and the adults listen for the request underneath.

passage:
In the kasba, everyone's children went to Sharma Sir's tuition near the bus stand. Hrithik had gone there for three years, and now Papa had paid for Mahima to join too.
"Why do I have to go where Hrithik went?" Mahima said at dinner. "That's not a reason. That's just habit."
Papa put down his roti. "It's a good centre."
"Says who? Three years and Hrithik still hates maths."
Hrithik snorted into his dal.
Papa's jaw tightened, then he looked at Mahima's face. She was gripping the steel glass too hard. "What's the real trouble?"
Mahima took a breath. "Sharma Sir calls the girls 'the back row' and never checks our copies. Rekha's didi goes to the new teacher near the temple. I want to try one class there."
Papa was quiet. "One class. We'll go together on Sunday and see."

qa.q: Where did everyone's children go for tuition?
qa.a: They went to Sharma Sir's tuition near the bus stand.

qa.q: What does Mahima's grip on the steel glass suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt tense and anxious, pushing past nervousness to argue with Papa. It could also show frustration that her real worry had not been heard yet.

qa.q: What would you advise a parent facing a challenge like Mahima's?
qa.a: Like Papa, pause before defending the rule and ask what the real trouble is, then offer a small, fair trial rather than a flat yes or no.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see his sister's challenge?
qa.a: Hrithik seems amused, and he may quietly agree, since his snort suggests the tuition has not helped him much either.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager disputing a family rule as she builds independence, and her father listening for the request underneath.

passage:
Under the floodlights of a wet pitch in Leeds, Coach Felix read out the Saturday team. Siddiq's name wasn't on it.
"That's not fair," Siddiq said, loud enough for everyone to hear. "Your rule about missing practice is wrong. It punishes people for stuff they can't control."
A couple of boys whistled. Felix held up a hand to them, then turned to Siddiq. "Go on. Why is it wrong?"
"Because some of us have other things. Tuesdays I can't come. That doesn't mean I don't care."
"What happens on Tuesdays?"
Siddiq kicked at the mud. "I pick my little sister up from school. Mum works late."
Felix nodded slowly. "Thanks for telling me. The rule was about commitment, not about punishing that. Come Thursdays, message me on Tuesdays, and we'll look at Saturday again next week."

qa.q: What does Siddiq do on Tuesdays?
qa.a: On Tuesdays he picks his little sister up from school.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq challenge the rule so loudly?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and angry at being left out of the team, and felt the rule judged him unfairly. Kicking the mud suggests he also felt a little embarrassed to explain his family situation.

qa.q: Which choice of Coach Felix's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking "Go on. Why is it wrong?" instead of shutting Siddiq down worked, because it brought out the real reason and let the rule be adjusted fairly.

qa.q: What would change if Felix had just told Siddiq to stop arguing?
qa.a: Siddiq would likely have felt unheard and more resentful, and Felix would never have learned about the Tuesday pickup.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager disputing a rule to stand up for himself and an adult listening for the request underneath the challenge.

passage: At the girls' hostel meeting, Deepika stood up before the warden had finished the notices. "Why do phones get collected at eight? We're not kids. It's a stupid rule and nobody has ever explained it." A few girls clapped. Someone at the back whispered, "She's done now." Irawati Ma'am put the register down. "Fair question. The rule is there so study hour stays quiet. What does eight o'clock cost you?" Deepika's chin was still up, but her voice dropped. "My father drives the night bus. He can only call at nine, on his break." The room went quiet. Irawati Ma'am wrote something in the margin. "Then that's the real request, and it's reasonable. Anyone with a family call after eight, give me the time. You'll get your phone for fifteen minutes, in the office." Deepika sat down, arms still folded, but nodding.

qa.q: When can Deepika's father call?
qa.a: He can only call at nine, on his break.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she called the rule stupid?
qa.a: Deepika was frustrated and probably worried about missing her father's calls. The raised chin also suggests wanting to be treated as grown-up, not only anger at the rule.

qa.q: How did Irawati Ma'am turn the challenge into something useful?
qa.a: She called it a fair question, gave the reason for the rule, then asked what it cost Deepika, which uncovered the real request and led to a fair fix.

qa.q: Why might the girls who clapped see the challenge differently from the warden?
qa.a: The girls who clapped likely saw a bold stand against a rule, while the warden listened for the need underneath and found a request she could meet.

grounding: It shows a teenager disputing a hostel rule as part of growing independence, and an adult listening for the request underneath the challenge.
